name: Escape to Host
description:
Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host. This can allow an adversary access to other containerized or virtualized resources from the host level or to the host itself. In principle, containerized / virtualized resources should provide a clear separation of application functionality and be isolated from the host environment.(Citation: Docker Overview)

There are multiple ways an adversary may escape from a container to a host environment. Examples include creating a container configured to mount the host’s filesystem using the bind parameter, which allows the adversary to drop payloads and execute control utilities such as cron on the host; utilizing a privileged container to run commands or load a malicious kernel module on the underlying host; or abusing system calls such as `unshare` and `keyctl` to escalate privileges and steal secrets.(Citation: Docker Bind Mounts)(Citation: Trend Micro Privileged Container)(Citation: Intezer Doki July 20)(Citation: Container Escape)(Citation: Crowdstrike Kubernetes Container Escape)(Citation: Keyctl-unmask)

Additionally, an adversary may be able to exploit a compromised container with a mounted container management socket, such as `docker.sock`, to break out of the container via a [Container Administration Command](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1609).(Citation: Container Escape) Adversaries may also escape via [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068), such as exploiting vulnerabilities in global symbolic links in order to access the root directory of a host machine.(Citation: Windows Server Containers Are Open)

In ESXi environments, an adversary may exploit a vulnerability in order to escape from a virtual machine into the hypervisor.(Citation: Broadcom VMSA-2025-004)

Gaining access to the host may provide the adversary with the opportunity to achieve follow-on objectives, such as establishing persistence, moving laterally within the environment, accessing other containers or virtual machines running on the host, or setting up a command and control channel on the host.

references.description: Broadcom. (2025, March 6). VMSA-2025-0004: Questions & Answers. Retrieved March 26, 2025.
Daniel Prizmant. (2020, July 15). Windows Server Containers Are Open, and Here's How You Can Break Out. Retrieved October 1, 2021.
Docker. (n.d.). Use Bind Mounts. Retrieved March 30, 2021.
Fiser, D., Oliveira, A.. (2019, December 20). Why a Privileged Container in Docker is a Bad Idea. Retrieved March 30, 2021.
Fishbein, N., Kajiloti, M.. (2020, July 28). Watch Your Containers: Doki Infecting Docker Servers in the Cloud. Retrieved March 30, 2021.
Manoj Ahuje. (2022, January 31). CVE-2022-0185: Kubernetes Container Escape Using Linux Kernel Exploit. Retrieved July 6, 2022.
Mark Manning. (2020, July 23). Keyctl-unmask: "Going Florida" on The State Of Containerizing Linux Keyrings. Retrieved July 6, 2022.

telemetry.name: Container Creation
telemetry.description: Creation of a runtime container object.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect runtime create events and image/container IDs; correlate with API audit to establish the initiating identity.

providers.name: Docker Engine events
providers.scope: Daemon lifecycle events for containers and images; collect continuously.

providers.name: Kubernetes API audit
providers.scope: Control-plane context in Kubernetes, not a replacement for runtime observations.

configuration: Subscribe to the lab daemon event stream with filters for the relevant object/action; send it to a durable collector.
Record runtime/container ID, image digest, action, timestamp and host. Join orchestrator identities where available.
Use a protected collector connection. Docker socket access is privileged; never expose it publicly or grant it to the website.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Runtime event history is bounded and can be lost without continuous collection. Image tags are mutable; pin digests. A lifecycle event is not a full process or file audit.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per workload image and namespace: rare process starts, unexpected image/privilege changes and new network relationships. Use workload/deployment identity, not short-lived container IDs alone.

telemetry.name: File Creation
telemetry.description: Creation or overwrite of a file at an observed path.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon FileCreate (11) to the lab directory; retain the process and file path. Differentiate creation/overwrite if the sensor can.

telemetry.name: Kernel Module Load
telemetry.description: Loading of code into the operating-system kernel as a module.
telemetry.collection_focus: On a Linux lab host, review Audit coverage for supported module-loading syscalls and correlate kernel module inventory; Windows driver-load collection is a separate option.

providers.name: osquery
providers.scope: Scheduled host-state queries; supported tables and privileges vary by OS. Select a table that actually exposes the required object.

providers.name: Linux Audit plus inventory snapshots
providers.scope: Events explain changes; snapshots describe state at collection time.

configuration: Define the inventory query, allowed host set, interval and least-privileged reader. Store a stable asset ID, observation time and collector version.
Keep successive snapshots and calculate additions, removals and changed attributes. Pair state changes with audit events when available.
Export collector health and missed-poll counts so a missing snapshot is not misclassified as a missing asset.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Snapshots miss short-lived objects and do not identify who caused a change. A generic inventory agent is not guaranteed to expose firmware or kernel-level details.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Compare authorized state snapshots: first-seen drivers/services/modules, unexpected configuration drift and integrity changes. Record collection cadence; absence in a sample is not evidence of deletion.

telemetry.name: OS API Execution
telemetry.description: Instrumented operating-system API calls and their return values.
telemetry.collection_focus: Use an approved EDR trace or instrument the owned lab process at selected APIs. Define API name, caller, sanitized arguments and return status.

providers.name: Application audit logs
providers.scope: First-party service events and request/result fields; schema is application-specific.

providers.name: OpenTelemetry-compatible log pipelines
providers.scope: Transport and normalization of emitted records; do not create missing audit instrumentation.

configuration: Enable the application audit category or instrument the owned lab application at the authorization/action boundary.
Define a schema with timestamp, service, actor, object, action, result and correlation ID. Export structured records through an authenticated collector.
Redact secrets and personal content, separate audit from debug logs, set retention and verify delivery during rotation/restart.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Debug output is not necessarily a durable audit trail. Application developers must emit the relevant event; installing a log pipeline does not make an absent event exist.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per application, client and route: request rate, rare actions, failure ratios and unusual state transitions. Version changes, retries, health probes and seasonal load need separate baselines.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Escape to Host

analytics.name: Analytic 0612
analytics.guidance: Detection of container escape attempts via bind mounts, privileged containers, or abuse of docker.sock. Defenders may observe anomalous volume mount configurations (e.g., hostPath to / or /proc), unexpected privileged container launches, or use of container administration commands to access host resources. These events typically correlate with subsequent process execution on the host outside of normal container isolation.

tuning.description: List of directories permitted for hostPath volumes. Any access beyond these paths may be suspicious.
Number of privileged container launches expected in the environment. Exceeding this may indicate adversary behavior.

log_sources.name: docker:daemon
log_sources.channel: container create/start with privileged flag or host volume mount

log_sources.name: kubernetes:apiserver
log_sources.channel: Pod spec with hostPath or privileged securityContext

analytics.name: Analytic 0613
analytics.guidance: Detection of Linux container escape attempts via syscalls (`unshare`, `keyctl`, `mount`) or process execution outside container namespaces. Defenders may correlate unusual system calls from containerized processes with subsequent process creation on the host or modification of host resources.

tuning.description: Expected syscalls by containerized workloads. Deviations may signal an escape attempt.
Defines correlation window (e.g., 60s) between suspicious syscalls and follow-on host process activity.

log_sources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
log_sources.channel: unshare, mount, keyctl, setns syscalls executed by containerized processes

log_sources.name: linux:Sysmon
log_sources.channel: process creation events linked to container namespaces executing host-level binaries

analytics.name: Analytic 0614
analytics.guidance: Detection of Windows container escape attempts by observing processes accessing host directories, symbolic link abuse, or privilege escalation attempts. Defenders may detect anomalous process execution with access to system-level directories outside of container boundaries.

tuning.description: Critical system paths containers should not access (e.g., C:\Windows, C:\ProgramData).

analytics.name: Analytic 0615
analytics.guidance: Detection of ESXi escape attempts by monitoring for anomalies in hypervisor logs such as unexpected VM operations, privilege escalation events, or attempts to load malicious kernel modules within the hypervisor environment.

tuning.description: Modules permitted in the hypervisor. Loading any module outside of this list may indicate compromise.

log_sources.name: esxi:vmkernel
log_sources.channel: VM exit/entry anomalies, unexpected hypercalls, or kernel module loading

software.name: Doki
software.description: [Doki](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0600)’s container was configured to bind the host root directory.(Citation: Intezer Doki July 20)

references.description: Fishbein, N., Kajiloti, M.. (2020, July 28). Watch Your Containers: Doki Infecting Docker Servers in the Cloud. Retrieved March 30, 2021.

software.name: Hildegard
software.description: [Hildegard](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0601) has used the BOtB tool that can break out of containers. (Citation: Unit 42 Hildegard Malware)

references.description: Chen, J. et al. (2021, February 3). Hildegard: New TeamTNT Cryptojacking Malware Targeting Kubernetes. Retrieved April 5, 2021.

software.name: Siloscape
software.description: [Siloscape](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0623) maps the host’s C drive to the container by creating a global symbolic link to the host through the calling of NtSetInformationSymbolicLink.(Citation: Unit 42 Siloscape Jun 2021)

references.description: Prizmant, D. (2021, June 7). Siloscape: First Known Malware Targeting Windows Containers to Compromise Cloud Environments. Retrieved June 9, 2021.

software.name: Peirates
software.description: [Peirates](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0683) can gain a reverse shell on a host node by mounting the Kubernetes hostPath.(Citation: Peirates GitHub)

references.description: InGuardians. (2022, January 5). Peirates GitHub. Retrieved February 8, 2022.

actors.name: TeamTNT
actors.description: [TeamTNT](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0139) has deployed privileged containers that mount the filesystem of victim machine.(Citation: Intezer TeamTNT September 2020)(Citation: Aqua TeamTNT August 2020)

references.description: Fishbein, N. (2020, September 8). Attackers Abusing Legitimate Cloud Monitoring Tools to Conduct Cyber Attacks. Retrieved September 22, 2021.
Kol, Roi. Morag, A. (2020, August 25). Deep Analysis of TeamTNT Techniques Using Container Images to Attack. Retrieved September 22, 2021.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.description: Ensure containers are not running as root by default and do not use unnecessary privileges or mounted components. In Kubernetes environments, consider defining Pod Security Standards that prevent pods from running privileged containers.(Citation: Kubernetes Hardening Guide)

references.description: National Security Agency, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. (2022, March). Kubernetes Hardening Guide. Retrieved April 1, 2022.

mitigations.name: Execution Prevention
mitigations.description: Use read-only containers, read-only file systems, and minimal images when possible to prevent the running of commands.(Citation: Kubernetes Hardening Guide) Where possible, also consider using application control and software restriction tools (such as those provided by SELinux) to restrict access to files, processes, and system calls in containers.(Citation: Kubernetes Security Context)

references.description: Kubernetes. (n.d.). Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container. Retrieved March 8, 2023.
National Security Agency, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. (2022, March). Kubernetes Hardening Guide. Retrieved April 1, 2022.

mitigations.name: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
mitigations.description: Remove unnecessary tools and software from containers.

mitigations.name: Application Isolation and Sandboxing
mitigations.description: Consider utilizing seccomp, seccomp-bpf, or a similar solution that restricts certain system calls such as mount. In Kubernetes environments, consider defining Pod Security Standards that limit container access to host process namespaces, the host network, and the host file system.(Citation: Kubernetes Hardening Guide)

references.description: National Security Agency, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. (2022, March). Kubernetes Hardening Guide. Retrieved April 1, 2022.

mitigations.name: Update Software
mitigations.description: Ensure that hosts are kept up-to-date with security patches.

candidates.name: Deploy container using nsenter container escape
candidates.description:
In this escape `kubectl` is used to launch a new pod, with a container that has the host pids mapped into the container (`hostPID:true`). It uses the alpine linux container image. It runs with privilege on the host (`privileged:true`). When the container is launched the command `nsenter --mount=/proc/1/ns/mnt -- /bin/bash` is ran. Since the host processes have been mapped into the container, the container enters the host namespace, escaping the container.

Additional Details:
- https://twitter.com/mauilion/status/1129468485480751104
- https://securekubernetes.com/scenario_2_attack/

candidates.name: Privilege Escalation via Docker Volume Mapping
candidates.description:
This test demonstrates privilege escalation by abusing Docker's volume mapping
feature to gain access to the host file system. By mounting the root directory
of the host into a Docker container, the attacker can use chroot to operate as
root on the host system.

candidates.name: Mount host filesystem to escape privileged Docker container
candidates.description:
This technique abuses privileged Docker containers to mount the host's filesystem and then create a cron job to launch a reverse shell as the host's superuser.
The container running the test needs be privileged.  It may take up to a minute for this to run due to how often crond triggers a job.
Dev note: the echo to create cron_filename is broken up to prevent localized execution of hostname and id by Powershell.

mount_device.description: Path to the device of the host's disk to mount

mount_point.description: Path where the host filesystem will be mounted

cron_path.description: Path on the host filesystem where cron jobs are stored

cron_filename.description: Filename of the cron job in cron_path

listen_address.description: IP address to listen for callback from the host system.

listen_port.description: TCP Port to listen on for callback from the host system.

simulation.prerequisites: Use disposable lab hosts and test accounts, explicit target allowlists, a clean snapshot, bounded egress and a restore plan. Review every candidate and dependency before any execution.

synthetic.purpose: Collection/parser contract exercise, NOT a positive example or detection of this TTP.
